title: When And Why You Should Leave Your Students Alone ents-alone/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin contrasts teachers who constantly hover, reteach, and redirect during independent work with those who step back and let students work through challenges on their own. He argues that hovering, whether out of necessity from weak lessons or habit, teaches learned helplessness and poor listening skills, while receding into observation mode signals real, durable learning. He describes the ideal classroom moment as one where no hands go up and the teacher feels the urge to disappear so as not to disrupt the 'hum of production.' The article criticizes an educational culture that over-emphasizes individual hand-holding at the expense of building ownership, arguing that spoon-feeding removes curiosity and original thought. Linsin closes with a call to gradually build up the amount of time students spend working independently, even if it starts with just a few minutes a day.
points: Constant teacher hovering during independent work fosters learned helplessness and weak listening skills.
A room where students are deeply immersed and don't look to the teacher for help is a sign of true, effective learning.
Micromanaging students by interrupting with hints and asides disrupts learning rather than supporting it.
Over-helping individual students limits their chances of building ownership, curiosity, and original thought.
Build independent work stamina gradually, starting with even just a few minutes of unsupported work time per day.
quotes: The picture of an entire class lost in their work is the most beautiful sight in teaching.
For some this is done out of necessity. Their lessons and classroom management skills aren’t strong enough to support their students through more than a few minutes of truly independent work.
Exceptional teachers, on the other hand, know that their effectiveness is tied to how well and how long their students are able to work without their direct input.

You know you’re on the right track when no hands go up in the air, no one looks in your direction, and you have an intense desire to become invisible—for fear of disrupting the tender hum of production coursing throughout the room.
In this day and age, far too much emphasis is placed on helping individual students and not nearly enough on empowering them to take ownership of their education.

To reverse this devastating trend, work on increasing the amount of time your students spend engaged, engrossed, and immersed in learning activities devoid of your hovering presence, even if in the beginning it’s only a few minutes a day
